title: Comancheros attempted to muscle into construction sites, inquiry hears
text:
Outlaw motorcycle gang the Comancheros tried to install union delegates at construction sites in Queensland and establish their own companies in the sector, an inquiry has heard.

Today Queensland's Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and misconduct in the construction industry heard Australia's intelligence agencies had received reports about the Comancheros in early May 2024.

Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC told the inquiry unnamed intelligence agencies had information the Comancheros had already installed union delegates on construction sites in Victoria.

Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC told the inquiry Victorian members of the Comancheros travelled to Queensland. (Supplied)

"The Comancheros had taken measures over the preceding 12 months to establish their own companies that could operate in the construction industry in Victoria, most particularly labour hire companies," he said.

"Victorian members of the Comancheros had travelled to Queensland in the months prior to May 2024 with the aim of achieving those two objectives in the state of Queensland as well.

"That is the installation of union delegates on construction sites in Queensland … and the establishment of their own linked companies operating in the construction industry in Queensland."

He said the intelligence wasn't union, site or contractor specific, rather it was a "general commercial push" by the Comancheros.

Alleged bikie threat

Inquiry into Queensland's CFMEU branch Queensland's CFMEU inquiry has heard three Melbourne men linked to the Comancheros bikie gang flew to Brisbane before one allegedly threatened a construction worker at a major government project.

Yesterday, the inquiry heard about an incident where three people with links to the Comancheros travelled to Queensland and one threatened a worker at the Centenary Bridge construction site.

Flight and phone records tendered to the probe into the CFMEU and construction sector revealed Bemir Saracevic, Krstomir Bjelogrlic and Mark Ahern arrived in Brisbane on June 5, 2024.

Mr Saracevic, known as Benji, was the former national president of the Comancheros and Mr Bjelogrlic was his business partner. Mr Ahern was a former treasurer for the gang.

Senior Comancheros bikie Bemir 'Benji' Saracevic. (Supplied)

It's alleged they were picked up by Gary Samuel, the head of HOST, the company providing security to the site.

BMD General Manager Rob Pickard told the inquiry Mr Samuel had told him the three men were simply social acquaintances from Victoria who had visited him and had no role with HOST.

Mr Gisonda said there were allegations the worker targeted, Cody Raymond, had been passing on information about security at the site by the CFMEU during a drawn-out dispute between the union and contractor BMD.

"The cost of this disruption was mounting up and they had very little options available to them," he said.

Mr Gisonda told the inquiry it wasn't just the CFMEU that bikie gangs had targeted.

He said companies with links to the Comancheros not only had enterprise agreements with the CFMEU in Victoria, but also the Australian Workers Union.

Commissioner Stuart Wood KC is leading the inquiry. (Supplied)

One agreement, signed in April 2025 between FSA Kerbs and Placement Pty Ltd and the AWU, was signed by Mr Bjelorgrlic and witnessed by Mr Saracevic's partner, Dani Saracevic.

Another company, Form Solutions Australia of which Dani Saracevic was the director, had signed an enterprise agreement with the CFMEU in Victoria in December 2023.

The hearing continues in Brisbane.

title: Ratchet straps used as 'makeshift' lifting loops in accident, expert says
text:
A national crane inspection company says images from a government-funded worksite in Glenroy, Albury, show a "severe breach" of safety protocols, after glass panels fell during a lift and seriously injured workers last week.

The ABC understands two heavy packets of glass panels fell from a crane onto the workers, leaving one man in his 20s in a critical condition at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

A second man in his 20s was taken to Albury Base Hospital with serious but stable leg and back injuries, and a third worker escaped with minor injuries.

The union, CFMEU, said the worker from crane company WA Pickles was critically injured and a Padel Concepts labourer sustained a leg fracture.

WA Pickles and Padel Concepts were contacted for comment.

SafeWork New South Wales said it responded to the incident, but it would not comment while inquiries were ongoing.

Three men were injured in a workplace accident near Albury. (ABC News Philippe Perez)

'Almost unbelievable disregard'

Samuel Ho, director of Cranes Australia, which conducts independent engineering inspections on crane safety and compliance, said the images showed standard cargo tie-down ratchet straps being used as "makeshift lifting loops" to move the panels.

"The images depict a severe breach of rigging and crane safety protocols," Mr Ho said.

Mr Ho said the straps in the images lacked the structural properties required to safely support a suspended load.

"It is comical in a dark sense because using basic transport tie-downs to crane-lift heavy materials reflects such a fundamental, almost unbelievable disregard for basic site safety and high-risk work licensing rules," Mr Ho said.

The glass frames that fell on the workers. (Supplied: CFMEU)

'Worker lives at extreme risk'

Mr Ho said certified synthetic webbing, or chain or wire-rope slings, should have been used for the lift, alongside safety latched hooks or rated shackles.

He said lifting equipment should have featured load-limit markings, appropriate protections on sharp edges and been attached to engineered lifting points.

"Bypassing certified gear to save time or effort inevitably leads to dropped loads and places worker lives at extreme risk," Mr Ho said.

'Entirely preventable'

The ABC understands the site was being developed for padel and futsal facilities and funded through NSW Sport and Recreation.

NSW Sport and Recreation declined to comment.

Karma Lord says the CFMEU is seeking more details. (Supplied: CFMEU)

The CFMEU said it had asked for crane inspection records, lift plans and other safety documents from companies involved in the project.

CFMEU New South Wales branch executive Karma Lord said the accident was "entirely preventable".

"A three-tonne glass pack with no rated lifting points should never have gone near a crane," she said.

title: El Niño loads the dice for more extreme fire conditions
text:
After historic fires marred Europe's summer, experts are cautioning against complacency ahead of Australia's warm season, with the fire risk increasing in most states and territories over the coming months.

The Australian and New Zealand Council for Fire and Emergency Services (AFAC) has released its latest seasonal outlook, which shows an increased risk of fire in areas across all jurisdictions, except for the ACT, this spring.

Below-average rainfall has increased the bushfire risk across most jurisdictions. (Supplied: AFAC)

The widespread impact is due to dry conditions in the country's east and increased fuel loads through parts of central and northern Australia.

"The variety of risk factors across different regions reinforces the need for communities to understand their local conditions and prepare early," AFAC CEO Rob Webb said.

"While some areas are facing an elevated risk of fire this spring, bushfires can still occur in regions with a normal seasonal outlook."

Soil moisture deficits have expanded across eastern Australia and intensified in Western Australia by July 2026. (BOM)

Increased fuel loads have elevated the fire risk across most of the Northern Territory, despite forecasts suggesting the region could see above-average rainfall in spring.

Rainfall is also expected to be higher than normal for most of Western Australia, but the fire risk is high in some areas due to above-average fuel loads and dry soil conditions.

Parts of Western Australia show a high chance of an unusually wet spring. (BOM)

Below-average rainfall has increased the bushfire risk across large parts of southern Victoria and eastern Tasmania, including Flinders Island.

South-east Queensland, north-eastern New South Wales and north-west South Australia are also looking at an increased chance of fires.

Will El Niño make the fire season worse?

Fears have been growing around what Australia's spring and summer will look like after the weather bureau declared an El Niño in June, which has the potential to become the strongest on record.

El Niño is linked to reduced rainfall, particularly in eastern Australia, and increased temperatures, mainly across the country's south. It often helps load the dice for more extreme fire conditions, and past events have contributed to some of the country's hottest and driest years on record.

But predicting what impact the climate pattern will have on Australia each year is notoriously difficult, because it's just one factor that influences weather conditions. There are other climate drivers, such as the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and Southern Annular Mode (SAM), that contribute.

Local sea surface temperatures and natural weather variability also play a role.

El Niño develops when ocean temperatures in the central Pacific are unusually high. The strength of El Niño, or why some reports have referred to it as a 'super El Niño' this year, merely describes its signal, which so far has been off the charts compared to usual.

The strength of El Niño, or why some reports refer to it as a 'super El Niño' this year, merely describes its signal, which has been unusually high for this time of year.

The last El Niño 2023-24 brought us the warmest winter–spring since records began in 1910, but how it may impact rainfall is less clear.

'Caution against complacency'

While rainfall was above average for parts of northern and central Australia last month, it was unusually dry across much of the country's west and sections of the east.

Temperatures were also warmer than average across most of the country, with that trend expected to continue throughout spring.

Before: Spring daytime temperature maximums are likely unusually high in Australia's south. . . After: Night-time temperatures are forecast to be unusually high across the whole country. . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE Spring daytime temperature maximums are likely unusually high in Australia's south. / Night-time temperatures are forecast to be unusually high across the whole country.

Models suggest a positive IOD could emerge before spring, which could exacerbate the impacts of El Niño.

A professor of pyrogeography and fire science at the University of Tasmania, David Bowman, said vegetation growth had been "prolific" in forests recovering from bushfires in 2019-20 and it would not take much for that to dry out.

"There's a lot of water in the landscape, and that's resulted in a lot of productivity, a lot of fuel," he said.

"If we were to go into a summer under this El Niño where we had what we call flash droughts, which is really strong heat waves, we can switch up landscapes into extraordinarily dangerous conditions.

"In eastern Tasmania, there's been a very sustained drying trend; we have had water, but basically it won't take much to nudge landscapes back into a deep drought."

David Bowman says climate change has exacerbated Australia's fire season. (Supplied: David Bowman)

Climate scientists have long warned that fire seasons across Australian states and territories will start earlier and persist longer due to climate change.

Professor Bowman said the extra heat associated with climate change was dangerous when combined with El Niño.

"Plants are very good at controlling their water use, but if you subject them to very strong heating, you can rapidly stress and dry out landscapes and make the landscapes available for high-intensity fires," he said.

"My instinct would be to caution against complacency about particularly forest fires."

Southern hemisphere warnings

Australia's fire season will follow a devastating summer across the northern hemisphere, marred by successive record-breaking heatwaves and extreme wildfires in Europe, the United States and Canada.

Firefighters across Europe have faced turbulent conditions during the northern summer, including near Porto Germeno, north-west of Athens. (AP Photo: Michael Varaklas)

Professor Bowman said Australia's differences in climate and geography meant it is not necessarily subject to the same fate, but the events reinforced that fire seasons are worsening.

Climate scientist caught up in Europe's 'dystopian' summer Stefan Rahmstorf was holidaying in southern France when he came face to face with the climate future he has tried to fight.

"We are much more advanced in terms of our capacity, but it also is a very good reminder, particularly what's happening in the US and Canada, who are very advanced in managing fire, that they're seeing fire seasons and fire behaviours that are just simply extraordinary," he said.

"I have every reason to believe that we will see equally extraordinary fires. If it's not this summer, it's certainly going to be in the next [...].

title: FIFA accused of 'management by fear' after key executive's sudden exit
text:
The head of Norwegian football has accused FIFA of fear tactics for the removal of a senior official who publicly opposed FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-withdrawn World Cup sell-off plan.

Lise Klaveness, the head of the Norwegian Football Federation since 2022, told the Associated Press that the firing of FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour was "unacceptable" and urged other senior leaders to resist potentially damaging orders.

Mr Lamour's exit on Tuesday (AEST) came 17 days after his statement to AP criticising Mr Infantino's $US20 billion ($28.1 billion) private equity project, which was withdrawn hours later.

FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, leaves soccer's governing body, weeks after publicly criticising president Gianni Infantino.

"Now he is thrown out and we are supposed to move on. It's unacceptable, it's management by fear," Ms Klaveness told the AP in a telephone interview, describing Mr Lamour as "the best football administrator I have ever met".

"Now we also have to call upon FIFA leadership and the administration to not submit to orders you know are not in the interests of football," Ms Klaveness added, especially targeting FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafström.

Ms Klaveness represented Norway 73 times as a player, is a judge in Oslo and an elected executive committee member at European football body UEFA.

She has built on her country's long-held reputation as a champion of good governance in soccer.

Last week the Norwegian federation's board called on Mr Infantino to resign and has backed a London-based NGO's formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators about his political ties to US President Donald Trump.

Mr Lamour was a long-time colleague of Mr Infantino, first when they were senior officials at UEFA from 2007-15. He was involved in Mr Infantino's campaign to be elected FIFA president in 2016 and moved two years ago from UEFA to oversee much of FIFA's operations in Zurich.

Infantino in crisis

Kevin Lamour (centre) said FIFA staff were "deceived" by the World Cup sell-off plan. (Getty Images: Richard Sellers)

With a reputation among the most trusted executives in the often murky world of global football politics, Mr Lamour's pointed criticisms of Mr Infantino's leadership intensified a crisis for the FIFA president.

A backlash from UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and north American soccer body CONCACAF was provoked by a secretive plan to sell future World Cup profits to investors led by Joshua Kushner.

A $4.2 billion investment to take a 20 per cent stake in a FIFA commercial spin-off was to fund offers of $20 million to each of its 211 national member federations.

They already effectively own the non-profit soccer body, which has multi-billion dollar reserves, and would have had a mid-September deadline to accept.

Mr Lamour's statement on July 31 spoke of FIFA staff being "deceived" by Mr Infantino's lack of openness over the now-failed sale and how they "deserve better than contempt and intimidation".

The French executive called on soccer leaders worldwide "to make the right decisions".

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he said at the conclusion of the statement.

"I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

'A firing situation'

Lise Klaveness with Gianni Infantino at last month's FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

Ms Klaveness said Mr Lamour's exit was "a firing situation, it's not a resignation", and suggested it was done as a result of Mr Grafström "obviously being pressured by the president".

FIFA didn't respond to a request for comment on Ms Klaveness's remarks.

In a statement, FIFA said it "thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future. No further comment will be made on the matter".

Mr Lamour did not immediately reply to an email seeking comment on Wednesday (AEST).

"His statement was necessary to kill the project," Ms Klaveness said of Mr Lamour's intervention.

" He said something that was obvious, that was very important that someone within the staff told us the story so that we knew it was not FIFA, as such, but one person. "

Mr Infantino held a meeting with senior management — minus Mr Lamour — in Rabat, Morocco on August 5.

Following that, FIFA issued a statement apologising for errors and said those managers who attended "reaffirmed their full support" for Mr Infantino's presidency.

"We all got reports in Morocco, we know it's a management of fear," Ms Klaveness said.

"It's not in football's best interests."

Until the uproar over Mr Infantino's "FIFA Forward Enterprise" proposal, he seemed sure to be re-elected unopposed next year in Morocco for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

Challengers have until November 18 to enter the contest.

Norway not discussing other candidates

Though UEFA and other critics of Mr Infantino want him ousted from the $6 million-per-year FIFA job, Ms Klaveness said any search for an opponent was not a talking point in Norway.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"We are not there at all and that is 100 per cent the truth," she said, adding that any candidate would have to be "very accountable to a governance structure that will not in four or five years just deteriorate".

Mr Infantino was appointed by UEFA in 2015 to a panel advising FIFA on reforms, in fallout from corruption scandals provoked by US federal investigations.

That group's recommendations limiting FIFA presidents to 12 years in office, plus limiting their executive powers and patronage all have retreated under Mr Infantino.

Ms Klaveness acknowledged FIFA members had been less "passionate about the details of governance" than Norway.

Mr Lamour also won praise and support from UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister, also a former player and now a university professor of governance in Wales, who lamented the "shabby events of the past weeks".

"Kevin's sacking seriously weakens FIFA's administration whilst undermining this unique opportunity to shift the culture at FIFA and to reset the organisation on sporting values, not simply commercial and financial ones," Ms McAllister said.

AP

title: Bush kids raise thousands for charities with 19yo bike ride fundraiser
text:
Once a year, traffic along the Flinders Highway at Prairie comes to a standstill as dozens of brightly coloured pushbike riders cross the road, their wheels kicking up the red dust.

Despite being a town of only 100 people, Prairie, about 340 kilometres south-west of Townsville, pulls out all stops for its annual bike-ride fundraiser.

The event is in its 19th year. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

For 19 years, the Tour De Prairie, run by the school, has raised thousands of dollars for charities important to members of the community.

School P&C treasurer Bernie Merton said about $1,000 was raised each year.

Participants rode or walked 7 kilometres to raise money. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

"I think it's really good, everyone enjoys it, and older boarding school kids come back for it and it's just nice to jump on a bike and go for a ride," she said.

This year, donations went to the Royal Flying Doctor Service (RFDS), with the event being held in memory of local boy Conall Wescott, who died in May from the rare genetic condition Gould syndrome.

The Westcott family took part in the event for their son Conall. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

Conall's father, Hugh Westcott, said the RFDS was vital in supporting his family.

"We had multiple flights to Townsville where they kept him alive, they saved his life numerous times," he said.

In memory of locals

Each year, students from Prairie State School choose a charity to raise money for.

In previous years, they have supported Cows for Cambodia, Cancer Council, and have raised money for the chemotherapy treatment room at the Hughenden hospital.

This year's theme was bright colours. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

Parents, teachers, students and the wider community ride their pushbikes 7km out to Railview cattle station, where they play games and eat lunch.

Some participants even rode the 7km back into town. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

Railview grazier Michelle Fryer has supported the cause since it started in 2007, when it raised money for the Cerebral Palsy Alliance, in memory of her daughter Alex.

"She's always in everyone's memory, there's memories of her at the school still," she said.

Alex died just days after her eighth birthday from complications of cerebral palsy.

"That was the first year and then, after that, we just said, 'It doesn't always have to be about Alex, it just needs to be somebody in need,'" Ms Fryer said.

" Prairie's a great community and it's just about giving back. "

Ms Fryer reflects on some memorable years of the fundraiser.

"Those first few years, there were a lot of flat tyres and the parents all started getting savvier."

She said she hoped to see it continue for years to come.

"We do it for the kids, and we're happy to keep doing it until the children don't want to."

The outback roads have caused a few flat tyres over the years. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

Caravanners supporting the cause

Ms Merton said the children received a lot of donations from tourists or people passing through town.

This year's Tour De Prairie was raising money for the Royal Flying Doctor Service. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

"It gives them confidence when they go around the caravan parks and ask the tourists and strike up a conversation," she said.

title: How chickens and cattle are a surprising fit in soil restoration
text:
Best known for its wide-open spaces, carpets of wildflowers and grazing cattle, Western Australia's Murchison region is an unlikely setting for the animated clucks and busy scratching of a small commercial chicken flock.

But on Gabyon Station, about 500 kilometres north-east of Perth, Gemma Cripps and Helen Williamson are discovering that chickens can do more than lay eggs: they also help restore small patches of rangeland soils.

The chickens live in a caravan at night, which automatically opens and closes on a timer. (ABC Mid West Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

For the past two years, the pair have run about 150 laying hens on their cattle property, keen to see if soil hydration and plant health could be improved by intensive chicken grazing.

"After doing a [regenerative agriculture] workshop we decided to try and see what impacts we could create on the land here, so we've been trying different things, and chooks is one of them," Ms Cripps said.

"The regenerative benefits we are getting are astounding.

"With the manure the chooks leave behind, and the way they scratch the dirt where they are grazing lets the water infiltrate and creates fertiliser for the soil.

"We've noticed where we've had chooks, the next year where the wildflowers come up they're a different colour; we can only put that down to changing soil pH.

Gemma Cripps and Helen Williamson had to replenish their flock numbers after a dingo attack earlier this year. (ABC Mid West Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

" There was more of a yellow-white [flower] base that changed to a pink. "

While the chickens are having a positive impact on the landscape, it seems nature is also affecting the eggs.

Following winter rain and a flush of green feed, Ms Cripps said the flock's yolks deepened to rich orange, but surprisingly, the chickens did not eat the wildflowers, preferring to scratch around them.

The eggs from Gabyon Station are sold in Geraldton. (ABC Mid West Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

With Gabyon spanning 271,000 hectares, the chickens reach a very small area of the station. But Ms Cripps believes they are a long-term fit on the property.

Dingoes and bird flu

While it sounds idealistic, the venture has not been without setbacks.

Earlier this year, a dingo attacked, killing about 80 chickens in a single morning and dealing a significant blow to egg production.

As a result, the chickens are now kept safe by a large, portable electric fence, which is moved frequently across a paddock.

A portable electric fence keeps the chickens safe. (ABC Mid West and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

In June this year, the highly pathogenic H5 bird flu strain was found in West Australian sea birds, posing a significant concern for the state's egg industry.

With Gabyon located 200km from the coast in an isolated area without a permanent water source, Ms Cripps hopes the distance will provide protection.

Gemma Cripps and Helen Williamson with their mascot Christine, whose shiny outfit is designed to keep birds away. (ABC Mid West Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"We want to keep the birds as a free-range operation; if we had to keep the animals contained, I'm not sure how we'd go about that," Ms Cripps said.

"[Authorities are] possibly looking at a housing order; unfortunately for us here, that would be very difficult, our quarantine procedure would probably be to cull the chickens."

But they are hoping for the best and moving towards breeding their own chickens for increased biosecurity.

Ms Cripps said if demand for eggs increased they would consider increasing their flock size, but any growth in flock numbers would need to cover increased feed and management costs.

Gabyon Station was historically a sheep station but has moved to cattle production. (ABC Mid West Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

title: Lawyers replace jockeys in 'chaos' of camel race
text:
In the remote opal mining town of White Cliffs, four lawyers and a builder prepare to do something few professionals would put on their resume: camel racing.

Most of them have never ridden a camel before, much less raced one.

As they strap on their helmets, they listen intently as a woman in denim flares and a cowboy hat explains how best to avoid falling off.

Spectators watch from the sidelines while volunteers ride camels down the track at the 2026 White Cliffs Camel Cup. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"When they're standing up, just hold on and lean back slightly," she says.

" And [above] everything else, just hang on for dear life. "

No experience, no worries

The annual Camel Cup is one of the outback's more unusual traditions, involving locals rather than professional jockeys.

Cup day involves six heats, all of them featuring volunteer jockeys.

In this particular race, five Broken Hill locals with no camel riding experience have varying levels of confidence.

Harry Fisher, a lawyer from Wollongong who moved to Broken Hill earlier this year, is one of the more self-assured racers and has his heart set on winning, except there is one small problem: he has never ridden a camel before.

Originally from Wollongong, Broken Hill lawyer Harry Fisher said he was in the race to win it. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"I'd heard a rumour a few weeks ago that people who come along get a chance [to race on a camel]," he says.

"As soon as I heard that, I thought, 'I just want to get involved in this camel racing.' I'm doing this for the story."

Competing against him is his friend and fellow lawyer Danyon O'Rourke, who has set the bar considerably lower.

"My main goal really is to stay on the camel," he says.

As the five racers climb aboard, it becomes clear that staying on might be easier said than done for Danyon.

The five riders had no racing experience but varying levels of confidence. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

His camel seems less than enthusiastic about the arrangement, repeatedly deciding, without warning, to sit down.

Felicity Forge, another lawyer who also only recently moved to Broken Hill, admits she came into the race without much of a strategy.

"I had absolutely no plan," she laughs.

"Just stay on, stand up."

Four lawyers and a builder from Broken Hill prepare to race on camels. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

Felicity had not planned on entering the camel race at all when she arrived at the Camel Cup.

"It was peer pressure, mostly," she says.

How to pick a winning ride

The race is just as much a gamble for spectators as it is for riders.

Auctioneer David Whittenbury encourages punters to place their bets on which camel will win — though he admits there is no secret formula for picking the winner.

"It's chaos, that's the only way to describe it," he says.

" It's all about the camel's desire. "

Camel Cup auctioneer David Whittenbury said there is no clear way to pick a winner. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

At least some of the riders attempt to devise a game plan.

Oliver Sinclair, also a lawyer, stretched in preparation while discussing his strategy with fellow rider Adam Collier, the only person in the heat who is not a lawyer.

"I'm going to serenade my camel … it's going to carry me home," he tells Adam.

For Danyon, however, the strategy is less about winning and more about getting his reluctant camel to the starting line.

Multiple attempts by camel handlers to coax his beast into moving prove unsuccessful as it repeatedly lies down in the middle of the track.

An auction is held to bet on who will win. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"[As] we walked to the starting line, the trainers were talking between each other and said they would take my camel back to the stables after my race," he says, presumably due to the animal's reluctance to participate.

These comments do not ease his doubts about his chances.

And they're racing

Eventually, the camels are ready to race.

The woman in flare jeans takes her cowboy hat off to signal the start, and spectators scale the fence to cheer the riders on as the camels charge past.

Immediately, Felicity and her camel cut away from the pack, taking a clear lead, while Danyon's camel seems to be facing in the wrong direction.

Felicity Forge, the newest to the region of the group, easily took out the win. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

Amid a cloud of dust, the camels lumber around the track, looking more awkward than athletic.

The race lasts about 30 seconds, with Felicity and her camel taking out the top spot.

After the race, Harry concedes he is disappointed with placing third.

"It was a hard-fought race," he says.

Harry Fisher and Felicity Forge celebrate after the race. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"I didn't win, but I didn't come last, that's the main thing."

Danyon, who did come last, may have been the real winner.

He achieved the only goal he had set himself: he stayed on.

Adam Collier, a builder from Broken Hill, placed second. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

More volunteer jockeys than ever before

The White Cliffs Camel Cup and Bikekhana has been running about five years, according to club secretary Honor Taylor, though previous events have not seen quite as many punters keen to climb aboard.

"In previous years, if you want to come and ride, you just sign a waiver and put your name down," she says.

Motorcyclists prepare to race in the White Cliffs bikekhana. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

" Normally, people get to have two or three races. But this year I just had too many jockeys — so many people wanted to come and have a go. "

After a slow start to tourist season across the region, Honor says the numbers who turned out for the race will have a huge impact on the community.

"We probably had about 650 through the gate," she says.

Riders took to the dirt for the bikekhana part of the event. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"It's a good boost to the town.

"We're probably about 90 per cent down on tourism, basically because of fuel prices and the cost of living, so these events boost up the town and businesses and accommodation."

Initially, the plan was to host the White Cliffs Bikekhana every year, with the camel races an addition to the event every second year.

But the races became so popular, they became an annual fixture.

A motorcyclist races through the dust in the White Cliffs bikekhana. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"We did camels and bikes and were going to do camels every second year, so the next year we just did bikes, and it wasn't as big or good," Honor says.

"So yes, it'll be an annual event … A lot of people have never seen them before … everyone loves it."

title: 'Marketing shame': What experts think about whole-body deodorants
text:
You may have noticed new deodorants at the supermarket or in social media feeds recently, with taglines such as "pits, privates and beyond".

These "whole-body" deodorants are raising eyebrows among some biologists, dermatologists and marketing researchers.

Data from the Australian Ad Observatory has recently highlighted the prevalence of the products, says Giselle Newton, a research fellow at the University of Queensland's Centre for Automated Decision Making and Society.

"This study asks Australians to identify all of the ads that they see in their feed in a 10-day period," Dr Newton says.

"And as part of that work, we did capture a number of these all-body deodorants."

She says the products are being advertised by both small and major cosmetic brands.

"[They're] being promoted in kind of traditional forms of digital advertising, but also in other forms of promotional content, like influencer content."

But do we even need whole-body deodorants and where on your body is it OK to use them?

Can our whole body sweat and stink?

Associate Professor Deshan Sebaratnam, a dermatologist from The Skin Hospital in Sydney/Gadigal lands, says body odour is caused by bacteria that live on the skin and feed on sweat.

But, he adds, "you have different sweat glands in your body".

"Apocrine sweat glands are found in the armpits and groin and these produce sweat that contains compounds which are broken down by bacteria and can contribute to body odour (bromhidrosis)."

The rest of your body is typically covered in eccrine sweat glands, he says.

" These mostly release water and electrolytes and so don't smell bad. "

Experts say "whole-body" deodorants are a new trend in cosmetic products. (ABC Lifestyle: Amy Sheehan)

However, Dr Sebaratnam says moisture from these glands can contribute to bacterial overgrowth in areas such as under the breasts or feet, and "this may smell unpleasant".

Our experts say if you are showering daily, these body odours will be under control in most cases.

Dr Naomi Koh Belic, a biology expert based in Sydney, on Gadigal lands, says eccrine sweat glands also serve an important function of cooling our body.

"We are meant to sweat, it's very important and helps regulate your temperature."

They're deodorants, not antiperspirants

A lot of the "whole-body" products are deodorants, not antiperspirants, and our experts say it is important to understand the difference.

Deodorants typically use antibacterial ingredients and perfumes to disguise odour.

"So, deodorant just kind of covers the smell," Dr Koh Belic says.

Everything you need to know about 'natural' deodorants There's a difference between deodorant and antiperspirant, for starters.

"Maybe there's a little bit of alcohol that might kill off some of the bacteria, but it's not really doing much to stop you from sweating."

Dr Sebaratnam says whole-body deodorants can contain ingredients that help to absorb moisture, "like silica, arrowroot powder, tapioca or cornstarch".

"The products don't stop you sweating per se, but the liquid is quickly absorbed and so don't have that wet sensation," he says.

Dr Koh Belic says that if you do experience body odour due to sweat, "you might prefer using antiperspirants".

She says antiperspirants work by blocking the output of sweat glands, "so that the sweat doesn't come out" and bacteria can't feed off it.

'Creating a problem where there isn't one'

While he says anything you apply to your skin could provoke an allergic reaction, Dr Sebaratnam believes all body deodorant products are mostly "innocuous".

Chris Callewaert, a microbiologist and sweat researcher based in Europe, says the "new trend" does have the potential to interfere with the skin microbiome.

Chris Callewaert says introducing a new product to certain areas of the skin can create issues. (Supplied: Dr Chris Callewaert)

The skin microbiome is the complex ecosystem of microorganisms including bacteria and fungi that protect against pathogens and maintain overall skin barrier health.

"The more antibacterial ingredients present in a skin cosmetic, the bigger the impact on the skin microbiome," says Dr Callewaert, who also goes by the name "Dr Armpit".

He says using the products "can lead to unwanted side effects, among which are odours, infections, rashes and sensitive skin".

Dr Koh Belic agrees and says the products may create a problem "that doesn't need to exist".

Using them in sensitive areas, like around your genitals, is not recommended.

Marketing 'shame and embarrassment' about bodies

Dr Newton believes cosmetic companies are "creating problems related to the body and health" and then selling solutions, "in this case deodorants".

"We know that sweat is a normal part of life, and body odour tends to occur alongside sweat," she says.

How social ads target women There's a big market online for products to put in or on our genital areas, blurring the lines between hygiene, cosmetics and medicine.

"But certainly, from an advertising and a social perspective, companies promote ideas to increase the shame and the uncertainty related to our bodies and our health."

She says encouraging the use of these deodorants with terms like "pits, privates and beyond" also creates a "vagueness and ambiguity" for consumers.

"It is misleading or encouraging [consumers] to engage in risky behaviours [such as using them on or near genitals] that could harm their bodies and their health."

Our experts say if you're worried about body odour or sweat, you should seek advice from a healthcare professional.

Dr Callewaert says the underlying cause of excess sweat and odour can be multifaceted and may include stress, diet, and hormones.

Dr Sebaratnam says it might also be a sign of a medical condition.

"Don't navigate it alone," he says.

" There are effective medical treatments for excessive sweating that impacts your quality of life. "

This is general information only. For personal advice, you should see a qualified medical practitioner.

title: Mother breaks silence as new details emerge in Hayden Panettiere's death
text:
Hayden Panettiere's on-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach were at the South Carolina apartment where the actor died over the weekend, according to a police report.

A Greenville police officer who went to the home on Sunday afternoon was met by the brothers and saw paramedics performing CPR on an unresponsive woman, the report released Tuesday, local time, said.

"The patient did not seem to have any obvious physical reasons to be unresponsive," the officer noted.

After attempting lifesaving measures, the emergency workers declared Panettiere dead.

In her final months, Hayden Panettiere chose to be 'brutally honest' The actress, who died on Sunday aged 36, spoke openly about the hardships she experienced throughout her decades in the spotlight.

No cause has been determined, and her death remains under investigation.

An autopsy found no signs of trauma, and police said officers saw no signs of foul play.

The one-time child star, who soared to fame in the TV shows Heroes and Nashville while enduring struggles with alcohol addiction and depression, would have turned 37 this week.

The report comes as Panettiere's mother, Lesley Vogel, spoke about the death, saying her daughter found herself on the wrong path.

"I think Hayden sadly lost her way, and I wish it were different," she told NBC.

"I wish she had stayed true to herself because she had many incredible attributes."

Before her death Hayden Panettiere said she was not speaking with her mother, Lesley Vogel. (Getty Images: Frazer Harrison)

In her 2026 memoir, Panettiere described a turbulent relationship with her mother, who she called a "perfectionist", and alleged that she had superglued a fallen tooth back into Panettiere's mouth so she would not lose a job.

Hickerson had history of abuse

The appearance of Brian Hickerson at the scene of Panettiere's death followed charges of abuse and a fraught relationship.

Hickerson was charged in 2020 with multiple counts of felony abuse and pleaded no contest to two counts of injuring a spouse or partner.

He served a short time in jail due to the case.

He was sentenced to four years of probation and anger management and Alcoholics Anonymous sessions.

He completed the terms and recently asked a judge to reduce his conviction to misdemeanours.

A Los Angeles judge denied that request Thursday.

US star Hayden Panettiere dies aged 36 Hayden Panettiere, star of Heroes and Nashville, has died. She was 36.

Panettiere wrote about Hickerson's time behind bars, saying she hoped it would change him.

"I needed him to admit his wrongs and change because of them, but I didn't want to traumatise him in an irreversible way," she wrote.

The police report on Panettiere's death, which is heavily redacted, said the responding officer first spoke with Zach Hickerson, who said the unresponsive woman was his brother's girlfriend.

"Brian did not become emotional until EMS declared her officially deceased," the officer said.

Also redacted is a list of medications that Panettiere had been taking.

Ex-fiance vows to share memory with daughter

In her book, Panettiere described lifelong scars from her early fame, and acknowledged being addicted to alcohol and enduring postpartum depression after the birth of her daughter, Kaya, with Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko in 2014.

Panettiere's daughter, now 11, began living with Klitschko full time in Ukraine when she was two.

At the time, the actor was struggling with her mental health and addiction.

She entered rehab in 2015 while filming Nashville.

Ex-fiance Wladimir Klitschko said Panettiere remained an "important part of my life". (Instagram)

Klitschko has also broken his silence, saying: "Nothing will erase the times we shared."

"To our daughter Kaya, I will always speak of her mother with respect and make sure she remembers the person she was," he shared on Instagram.

Panettiere had endured numerous family struggles and tragedies.

Her parents' marriage was strained and eventually ended.

Her younger brother, Jansen Panettiere, who was also an actor, died of a heart condition in 2023 at age 28.

Hollywood has continued to mourn the star's shocking death, with her director in Ice Princess paying tribute to its dual protagonists.

Panettiere starred in the 2005 Disney film alongside Michelle Trachtenberg, who also died in February last year, aged 39.

"I remember them both with huge affection, how they were 20-odd years ago, at that relatively uncomplicated time of their lives," director Tim Fywell told Variety.

" Two shining talents gone far too soon. "

AP/ABC

title: Dees star's ban upheld as AFL tribunal rejects biomechanist evidence bid
text:
Melbourne has suffered a major pre-finals blow, potentially losing key forward Jacob van Rooyen for the rest of the AFL season through suspension.

The Demons failed in their bid to have van Rooyen's three-game ban for striking overturned or reduced.

It means he will miss the fifth-placed Demons' final home-and-away game on Saturday against the Western Bulldogs, and that Melbourne will need to win two finals for him to play again this season.

Van Rooyen is having a career-best season, kicking 42 goals in 22 games.

The Demons forward was charged with striking after he concussed Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir in a marking contest on Saturday night at the Adelaide Oval. It was graded as severe impact, careless conduct and high impact.

After the 90-minute hearing, where van Rooyen testified that he was trying to mark the ball when he collected Aliir, the tribunal jury deliberated for nearly an hour before upholding the charge.

Melbourne had argued van Rooyen's attempt to mark the ball was not careless, but the tribunal rejected their case.

Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC also turned down a bid from the Demons to have a biomechanist give evidence for van Rooyen.

Aliir Aliir was left concussed after being struck in the head by van Rooyen's swinging arm. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

"The swing of van Rooyen's left arm constituted the act of a strike. It was a forceful blow. It was not simply a trailing or leading arm that Aliir collided with," Gleeson said in the verdict, adding the panel found it was careless.

"Van Rooyen was initially intending to mark the ball, but we find that shortly before impact, he ceased to intend to mark the ball. We say this despite van Rooyen's evidence to the contrary.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Even if it was van Rooyen's sole objective at all times to contest the mark, we find that he did so in a way that failed to take reasonable care to avoid acts which could be reasonably foreseen to result in a reportable offence.

"Van Rooyen had time to move his right arm in response to seeing Aliir and he could have done so to some extent or sufficient extent with his left arm."

The tribunal also found the impact was severe and said there was potential for further injury, such as a facial fracture.

Also on Tuesday night, Brisbane AFLW key forward Dakota Davidson failed to have her one-game striking ban downgraded.

The Lions pleaded guilty and tried to argue the clash with Essendon's Maddi Gay was low rather than medium impact, but the AFLW tribunal upheld the grading.

It means one of the league's top forwards will miss the grand final rematch against two-time defending premiers North Melbourne.

AAP

title: Accidental fire destroys family home in South West WA
text:
A family is lucky to be alive after a fire decimated their home in Western Australia's South West and destroyed everything they own.

Lisa Fawcett was asleep at the Boyup Brook house, about 260 kilometres south of Perth, on Sunday morning when a fire ignited.

While an official cause of the fire has not been determined by the Department of Fire and Emergency Services (DFES), Ms Fawcett said she believed a bar heater was left too close to a couch.

"I had everything I needed, and now I have nothing," she said.

"It's hard to comprehend."

The blaze destroyed the Boyup Brook home. (Supplied: Neil Wakeford)

'I just had to get out'

Ms Fawcett said she was woken by her son, whose room was the first to be filled with thick black smoke.

Still in her pyjamas, she rushed to grab her car keys.

Lisa Fawcett says it has been hard to comprehend the incident. (Supplied: Lisa Fawcett)

"All I could see was red flames," she said.

"By the time I was able to walk across the lounge room, the whole ceiling was just this really thick, choking black smoke."

As she walked towards the verandah to get the keys, she said the glass exploded around her.

"That's when I knew I didn't have time to grab anything, I just had to get out," she said.

Meanwhile, Ms Fawcett's son went to collect belongings from his room.

"It was too late, and he had to jump out the window to escape the fire," she said.

Emergency services were called to the property just after 10am on Sunday.

Ms Fawcett, who has narcolepsy, said she was in shock.

"It was just so quick. It was like three or four minutes to get to the reality of what was actually happening," she said.

"I have trouble waking up … that made it harder for me to even think what to do."

Irreplaceable loss

Ms Fawcett said her house was underinsured, but a payout would likely be enough to clear the site of debris.

But she said the sentimental possessions lost to the fire hurt the most.

Emergency services say a cause has not yet been determined for the non-suspicious fire. (Supplied: Neil Wakeford)

"I lost my partner seven years ago, so all the engagement rings and personal things and photos of him and that, I don't have anything," she said.

"Fifty years of collections and just all the antiques and grandma's jewellery and stuff like that is all gone."

During the fire, neighbours helped disconnect gas bottles and move her car.

Neighbours helped to save the family car during the incident. (Supplied: Lisa Fawcett)

Since the incident, Ms Fawcett said she had been offered temporary accommodation in Bridgetown.

"The community has been really supportive," she said.

South West Acting Superintendent John Bouwman said the fire was seemingly caused by a heater.

"As far as we know at this stage, it was caused by an electrical fault with a heater, or the heater was too close to some fabric [and] caused the house to go up," he said.

Acting Superintendent Bouwman said it was a relief the family managed to escape relatively unscathed.

"The injuries were more smoke-related, not [major] burns as such, is my understanding, so that's a good result," he said.

title: Venus Williams receives US Open wildcard at 46, Serena may follow
text:
Venus Williams has received a US Open singles wild card and the tournament is keeping one on hold, perhaps in case her sister Serena wants to join her.

Sloane Stephens, the 2017 US Open champion, was one of six other women to receive a wild card, and the US Tennis Association said the final one was still to be announced.

That will almost certainly go to Serena Williams if she decides she wants to return to the tournament at 44.

Venus Williams received a wild card last year, returning to the grand slam event she won twice for the first time since 2023. The 46-year-old has become the oldest entrant in singles at the tournament since Renee Richards played at 47 in 1981, according to the International Tennis Federation.

Serena Williams could make her return to Flushing Meadows via the final wildcard spot. (Getty Images: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport)

She has continued to play some singles matches, and this week joined Serena for their first doubles tournament together since the 2022 US Open. They lost at the Cincinnati Open in a match tiebreaker against Marta Kostyuk and Peyton Stearns.

The sisters planned to play at Wimbledon but had to withdraw after Serena injured her knee in her singles match. That marked her first time playing singles since the 2022 US Open, and she indicated afterwards that she hoped to keep competing if she was healthy.

Headlining the wild-card recipients on the men's side are 39-year-old Gael Monfils, a past US Open semifinalist who is set to play his final grand slam tournament before retiring, and Australian Alexei Popyrin, who upset Novak Djokovic in 2024 on the way to the fourth round.

One spot is also being held among the eight men's wild cards. Stan Wawrinka, the 2016 champion at Flushing Meadows, who at 41 is playing his final season, could be a candidate for that.

Australia's Alexei Popyrin has received one of the wildcards in the men's draw. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/David Kirouac)

Also receiving women's wild cards were Carol Young Suh Lee, Reese Brantmeier, Thea Frodin, Leolia Jeanjean and Taylah Preston.

The other men receiving wild cards were two-time reigning NCAA singles champion Michael Zheng, Martin Damm, JJ Wolf, Sebastian Gorzny and Jack Kennedy.

Kei Nishikori, the 2014 US Open runner-up who also is retiring, was given a wild card into the men's qualifying tournament, along with Jordan Lee, Trevor Svajda, Andre Ilagan, Spencer Johnson, Michael Antonius, Andrew Johnson and Daniel Milavsky.

Women given spots in the qualifying tournament were Caroline Dolehide, Janae Preston, Katrina Scott, Ayana Akli, Annika Penickova, Julieta Pareja, Kristina Penickova and Savannah Broadus.

The main draw begins on August 30, with the qualifying tournaments being played earlier that week.

title: Parent says primary schools don't teach computer skills like they used to
text:
When Emily Lockwood was at primary school, she would sit in a computer lab and learn how to type on a keyboard, make a presentation or save a file.

But for her two children, there are no such classes.

"Kids don't have that these days," Ms Lockwood said.

"Teachers are expected to weave digital learning throughout all of the subjects, so it might come up in History, Science, English, and that's a crazy ask to me."

While her children have grown up around devices, when they first attempted typing on a computer, it did not come naturally.

"It's pretty horrific to look at, it is like very slow, they're unfamiliar with where things go," she said.

Learning paper-based writing and computer skills were part of Ms Lockwood's primary education. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

She compared it to being in the back seat of a car, rather than knowing how to drive.

"People think they've grown up with this tech, they must be used to it, but it's not always the case."

'Keyboarding automaticity'

Ms Lockwood's children can bring their own device to school starting in year 3, as part of the government's optional Bring Your Own Device program.

But despite devices often being introduced to the classroom in the early years of primary school, research shows children still produce higher-quality writing by hand than when typing on a computer.

Primary school students are lacking computer skills. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Edith Cowan University senior education lecturer Anabela Malpique suggested this was because children had more experience writing by hand than typing on a computer.

"If you don't develop your keyboarding automaticity to a point where you actually are not hunting and pecking the letters on a keyboard, you will end up in a position of not really focusing on your ideas," Ms Malpique said.

To achieve this, explicit teaching of basic computer skills is required, just as with basic reading, writing and maths.

"They need to be told and taught how to actually engage with the computer to compose a text as opposed to discovering it," Ms Malpique said.

Ms Malpique says basic computer skills should be specifically taught just like other subjects. (Supplied: Anabela Malpique)

However, when students reach year 5, they are expected to sit their NAPLAN tests on a computer.

The tests were computerised for year 5, 7 and 9 in 2022, with year 3 students continuing to take written tests.

'Can't blame our teachers'

Following the release of this year's results, NSW Minister for Education and Early Learning, Prue Car, said computerised testing may be impacting writing results.

More than 77 per cent of year 3 students scored in the "strong" or "exceeding" categories for writing. However, that number dropped to 67 per cent in year 5 and continued to decline throughout high school.

By year 9, just over 61 per cent of students were classified as "strong" or "exceeding" in writing.

Developing keyboarding automaticity is key, says one expert. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Ms Car said she asked the federal Department of Education to "have a look at" moving the writing element of NAPLAN back to pen and paper for all year levels.

She said it might be influencing when schools chose to integrate technology, which was a decision left up to individual principals.

"We can't blame our teachers for wanting to get our students prepared for that computer-based test by introducing computers earlier," Ms Car said.

Ms Car says principals decide when to include technology. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

But Ms Malpique said even if this was the case, teachers reported spending more time and attention teaching paper-based writing skills, according to two national surveys she conducted.

"Teachers told us this happens either because they don't have enough training to teach computer-based writing, or they don't have the capacity in their schools to teach it," she said.

Computer-based writing research

The cognitive benefits of learning handwriting are strongly supported by evidence, with experts agreeing there is "something special" about using pen and paper.

Handwriting is still crucial for learning in digital world, experts say Most of the learning done in schools these days is digital. What does that mean for pen and paper and the art of handwriting?

But Ms Malpique said research into what was best for children when engaging in computer-based writing was scarce.

"There is a lack of developmental research, looking at the different stages of writing development," she said.

For Ms Lockwood, it feels like there is a gap between the importance placed upon technology in her children's education and the informal way it is introduced to their learning.

"We've decided this is really important and so there should be a dedicated space for it and a dedicated teacher for it."

title: NT Health issues urgent call-out for dozens more hospital workers
text:
The head of the Northern Territory Health Department has issued an urgent call-out for almost 60 qualified health workers to relieve frontline staff under "immense pressure" at the Darwin and Palmerston hospitals.

In a sector-wide email sent on Tuesday, seen by the ABC, NT Health acting chief executive Susan Bowden called for expressions of interest from qualified nurses, midwives and pharmacists in the NT to take on up to two weeks of duties at Royal Darwin Hospital (RDH) and Palmerston Regional Hospital (PRH).

It comes as the two Top End hospitals have been in a code yellow — called when extraordinary levels of patient demand lead to emergency procedures being put in place — since July 31.

It is the sixth code yellow to be called at the hospitals since January.

Susan Bowden says relieving fatigued staff is the "number one priority". (ABC News: Tilda Colling)

In her email, Ms Bowden said high demand had led to the hospital's frontline staff being put under "immense pressure" and as a result, "fatigue had set in".

"Reducing the pressure on RDH and PRH and providing our staff with respite is my number one priority. As such, I'm calling on those who can help out to do so where possible," she said.

She said the department was seeking up to 57 qualified workers, including 20 emergency nurses, to take up redeployment to the hospital floor, from other areas of the health sector.

The latest code yellow at RDH has been in place for more than two weeks. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

In a statement last week, an NT Health spokesperson said the department was investigating measures to relieve pressure, including a potential early opening of RDH's new 32-bed ward.

"We are throwing all of our resources and energy into this," Ms Bowden said in her email today.

Better conditions needed to fix long-term understaffing: union

Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation (ANMF) NT branch secretary Heidi Crisp said frontline nurses were increasingly feeling the current code yellow "is the worst one we've ever had".

"They just want the public to know how desperate times are," she said.

Heidi Crisp says better pay and conditions are needed to address the staffing issues at RDH and PRH. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Ms Crisp said the ANMF welcomed NT Health's call-out for surge workers, but warned it could lead to shortfalls in other departments.

Nurses claim staff use ChatGPT for medication doses Understaffing at the Northern Territory's busiest hospital is forcing nurses to take on what whistleblowers say are unsafe patient loads.

"In ED [the emergency department] we've seen high-level nurses being on the floor I think most of the year," she said.

"People are telling me it's about 25 per cent of this year we've been in code yellow … so if those nurses are taken from their desks to do other work, it means all of that background work can't be done, and that has a big effect on the system."

The union representative said the ANMF's NT members had voted down the Territory government's latest offer in enterprise bargaining negotiations, but that improved pay and conditions would improve staffing levels at NT hospitals in the long-term.

"Right now, tempers are really high [and] members are outraged at the offer that they've been given," she said.

"[The NT government] need to have a really hard look at what we have put in our log of claims, and really consider those pay and conditions that we have requested."

title: Live: Liberal senator to cross floor on gambling ad bill
text:
A vote is currently underway in the lower house on the government's news bargaining incentive legislation.

Labor needs to get the support of either the Greens or the Coalition to get the bill through parliament.

The legislation aims to ensure media outlets are paid if their content is used on platforms like Google and Facebook.

Labor is expected to move amendments to the legislation today, so the levy sits at 2.75 per cent of a tech company's ad revenue instead of the 2.5 per cent initially proposed.

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino told ABC Radio National Breakfast this morning that the increase was a good outcome for Australian media.

"What we have is a very balanced package," he said.

"A package that is sensible when it comes to the way in which we charge big tech, but also charges at an appropriate rate for Australia's media to make sure they get back into the position they were in in terms of the overall level of deals. "I am confident that we will have the support of both the opposition and the Greens in this package."

Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson said increasing the charge from 2.5 per cent to 2.75 per cent was an "appropriate amendment".

"We have raised concerns that as the bill was presented in the parliament, it took media organisations backwards — not forwards," she said.

"We are certainly very pleased that the charge is being increased.

"We certainly are supportive of the bill and particularly now that the charge has been increased, but let's just see what happens on the floor of the Senate in the coming days."

title: More women being diagnosed with POTS but rural patients face extra toll
text:
Piper Makin was living the typical life of a rural teenager.

Netball on weekends, high school during the week and helping her parents on the family farm at Keith, in South Australia's South East, was the schedule for the then-15-year-old.

But over a period of months, her energy and health started declining until she was spending days in bed and using a wheelchair to get around.

After pushing local doctors and hospitals for answers, one simple test showed Piper had postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, commonly known as POTS.

"I froze because I was so scared I was never going to be able to do fun things and activities like my sport and netball and all," she said.

As Piper Makin's health worsened, she spent much of her time on the couch and needed a wheelchair to get around. (ABC South East SA: Elsie Adamo)

"It's very hard to explain because people don't know what POTS actually is, so you just kind of have to give like all your symptoms and all of that and what you actually feel.

" I just got this feeling of no-one's ever going to believe me because they can't physically see what I'm going through. "

Limited research

POTS is a condition that affects the autonomic nervous system, the system that regulates essential functions such as our heart rate, breathing and digestion.

Chronic conditions dismissed as anxiety, low iron Young women have detailed their experiences being dismissed and misdiagnosed as chronic pain sufferers. Now, they're teaching others how to advocate for their health.

The Australian POTS Foundation says people between the ages of 15 and 50 are the most likely to develop the condition, with women at a far higher risk than men.

Symptoms are wide-ranging and different in each person, with Piper's including drops in blood pressure and general feelings of fatigue.

"You just want to rest all day, which is what I do," Piper said.

"It's kind of hard because once you rest all day, then you stand up and you feel like shit."

Rosemary Bryant AO Research Centre senior research fellow Marie-Claire Seeley said research on POTS had been limited, which left patients and families often without answers.

Marie-Claire Seeley says POTS remains misunderstood despite recent research findings. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

She said the condition was previously believed to be exclusively for young women who would later "grow out of it".

"That was because they didn't actually follow them for any time," Dr Seeley said.

" But we've just had a 20-year release of a paper where they followed POTS patients for 20 years that showed only 2 per cent recovered. "

Dr Seeley said a national survey of more than 2,000 general practitioners across Australia showed only 2 per cent had received any training in POTS diagnosis or treatment.

"They're women in the prime of their life, child-bearing time, work time, education time, who are just being withdrawn from the system silently," she said.

Piper and her mum Kylie Makin fought to find an answer to Piper's medical questions. (ABC South East SA: Elsie Adamo)

"Their families are having to manage the best they can with almost no support from our health system."

Finding community

About 800,000 people live with POTS in Australia, but with Piper living in a small regional community, knowledge of the condition was scarce and she knew no-one else with it.

Her mother, Kylie Makin, started documenting Piper's journey on Facebook, calling out for information and to raise awareness.

"It's hard because POTS can be so debilitating and even though she looks healthy, and she's such a pretty girl, Piper, it's hard then for people to understand she's so sick," she said.

Kylie Makin took to Facebook to try to better understand Piper's condition. (ABC South East SA: Elsie Adamo)

"I just had another phone call that there is another local girl over towards Bordertown that has POTS.

" So we're going to try and connect our two girls, at least then they can talk and network together and they know what they're feeling. "

What is POTS? And how is it related to long COVID? POTS or "postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome" is a poorly recognised condition that causes debilitating symptoms, and is very common among long COVID patients.

Ms Makin said the early days following Piper's diagnosis were both expensive and mentally draining, particularly living about 225 kilometres from Adelaide.

The family managed to find a doctor in Adelaide and started six weeks of intravenous (IV) injection therapy.

"That put a big pressure [on us], especially [when] we were going through the hardest, driest time on the farm," Kylie said.

"Leaving the farm and putting money in to help Piper get her back to where she needed to be."

Managing the future

Piper has been able to return to school and to the netball court, but managing the condition comes with varying bouts of progress and regression.

After treatment helped alleviate her symptoms, she was selected to participate in a netball carnival in Adelaide, but then had to pull out when she experienced a flare-up.

Piper Makin has returned to school and sport, but it means careful management of her symptoms. (ABC South East SA: Elsie Adamo)

Ms Makin hopes increased visibility of her daughter's condition will help others push for answers when they notice their health declining.

"If I wasn't very active in pushing for Piper, we'd probably still have her in a wheelchair," she said.

"We just don't have the awareness and we just don't have the facilities we can easily get to, so it does just make it tricky."

title: China’s breakneck plan to safeguard its future
text:
Advertisement

BusinessThe economyGlobal economy Opinion China’s breakneck plan to safeguard its future

Ambrose Evans-Pritchard August 19, 2026 — 11:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

China is about to do to the global supply chains for grains, livestock and food products what it has already done to the world’s energy and transport systems. The country is pursuing what amounts to world dominance in the mass manufacture of protein, launching a breakneck plan to end its strategic dependence on food imports and insure its people against the long-term famine risks of climate change. China has a plan to future-proof its food supply. Bloomberg The Politburo’s 15th five-year plan is marshalling all levers of finance and state power to overcome land and water limits, placing food security on a par with defence as an existential imperative for national survival. Analysts at consultancy Systemiq say the Communist Party is activating the same playbook already used for solar power, electric vehicles and batteries to reach 70 per cent or more of the world market from a standing start in less than 15 years – a pattern also visible in its push for semiconductors, nuclear fusion, quantum computing and pharmaceuticals.

Advertisement

It is developing genetically modified seeds and crops, but it is also targeting the fast-growing industries of cellular agriculture, lab-grown proteins and food from precision fermentation: Frankenfoods to some, the saviour of humanity to others. Related Article China relations China is dominating the EV market. Now it wants to do the same with robots Systemiq foresees a protein revolution picking up speed through the 2030s and 2040s that will radically change what the Chinese people eat, with spillover effects across Asia and the world. It estimates that half of China’s fish and beef consumption, and 40 per cent of its dairy products, will come from “alt-protein” sources by the mid-century. The country’s leaders have fretted about their food vulnerability for a long time. China has 15 per cent of the world’s population, 8 per cent of its arable land, and 6 per cent of usable freshwater – and some of that is badly polluted with nitrogen. The Sino-American struggle for global hegemony and the risk of a future US maritime blockade has brought matters to a head. So has the frightening pace of climate damage to Chinese agriculture. The country is now acting fast to future-proof itself for a Hobbesian “three-degree” world.

Advertisement

A throbbing hive of “doctoral farms” and technology courtyards has sprung to life in the Pinggu valley north-east of Beijing, best known for its blanket of pink peach blossom in late spring. It is billed as China’s second Silicon Valley, an agricultural tech (ag-tech) twin to the digital-tech hub at Haidian on the other side of the city. Other enzyme and amino acid hubs with different niches are being developed in the Yangtze River Delta and Guangdong. “It suggests a shift from isolated pilots towards a coordinated industrial ecosystem. This geographic clustering mirrors patterns observed in solar manufacturing and EV production during their pre-scale phases,” said Systemiq. Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. The battle for global supremacy between the US and China has accelerated Beijing’s plans. Getty The Pinggu nerve centre has begun making proteins for commercial use from micro-algae, as well as EPA fish oil and paramylon which is used in protein bars and cereals. The question of how soon climate change will erode global food output is a contested debate. The “CO² fertilisation effect” of higher carbon levels has until now been a net plus for crop yields due to faster photosynthesis and reduced water loss via stomatal conductance.

Advertisement

A Royal Society study last year concluded that we have passed the tipping point where friend turns to foes. The carbon dioxide benefits flatten out while the damage from heat stress and degradation of nutrients bites harder. Related Article Nutrition Whey protein is running out as food companies put it in everything Scientists from the US, Europe and China concluded in a seminal Nature paper that global crop yields are likely to be 8 per cent lower by 2050 than they would otherwise have been, even after adjusting for plausible ways of adapting. But we don’t know for sure and the process will not be linear. China’s Pinggu hub has a long way to go to catch up with the Wageningen “food valley” in the Netherlands, the world’s leading ag-tech hub, but the Dutch have recently been hobbled by a raft of anti-innovation EU rules that are driving some of Europe’s food-technology start-ups into exile. Several are migrating to the pro-science haven of Brexit Britain. What the Chinese lack in frontier biosciences – for now – they can more than compensate with vast industrial scale and state-directed credit. Systemiq thinks this could slash the cost of bioreactors and fermentation systems, achieving “price parity” with traditional food far sooner than widely supposed.

Advertisement

Once alt-protein is cheaper, market forces will make it almost unstoppable, in much the same way that 99 per cent of net electricity added across the world last year came from solar and wind. Food is not a mere commodity, of course. It goes to the heart of cultural identity and cuisine. It has a primal hold on our brain circuitry. So let me try to separate my analytical view from my personal tastes. On my farm we make cheese, kefir and whey from a herd of goats that roams at will over land that has been free of chemical pollutants for a very long time, eating whatever they want, much like their wild forebears in the Zagros mountains of Iran. Peach blossom in the Pinggu district of China. Alamy Stock Photo We never touch the processed foods that line the aisles of modern supermarkets. But large numbers of people do consume such products as a way of life and I doubt they would even notice whether lab-grown protein or milk made by precision fermentation crept into the ingredients. How many would rebel if “bio-identical” cultivated protein and lipids started to make up 10 per cent and then 20 per cent of a minced beef patty, a chicken nugget or a fish cake?

Advertisement

As a rule of thumb, it takes about 40 per cent less energy, 85 per cent less water and 95 per cent less land to make milk, from the gene coding of a cow, in a bioreactor vessel. It is not what I would drink by preference. But it could hardly be worse than the milk made from grain-fed cows imprisoned, 10,000 or 20,000 at a time from birth to death, in giant agro-industrial barns in China or the US, with little or no grazing in their miserable lives. The Sino-American struggle for global hegemony and the risk of a future US maritime blockade has brought matters to a head. China was a net exporter of crops and livestock as recently as 2004, before the shift to a high-protein diet led to soaring reliance on imported grains for animal feed. Today, Chinese demand sustains the grain export business of the western hemisphere, absorbing 89 per cent of Argentina’s soybean exports, 71 per cent of Brazil’s and (pre-Trump) 54 per cent of America’s. It buys most of Latin America’s beef exports. China’s food deficit has reached $US150 billion ($211.7 billion) a year.

Advertisement

These figures are going to plummet. The country is working on every front towards food self-sufficiency, pushing the growing frontier 200 kilometres north and deep into the Xinjiang desert with modified crops. It is reclaiming 37 million hectares of saline-alkali land by leaching out the salt. It has belatedly launched a “rural revitalisation strategy” after decades of neglect, finally treating farmers as a precious resource rather than cheap migrant labour for the cities. China was a net exporter of crops and livestock as recently as 2004, before the shift to a high-protein diet led to soaring reliance on imported grains for animal feed. Bloomberg But the ag-tech drive at Pinggu is the real wild card, with the potential to flood the teeming cities of the Global South – and not just the South – with cut-price protein and profoundly alter the contours of world food trade. Readers may prefer to stick to our organic cheeses, grass-fed Angus and stone-baked bread – and nobody will stop us, thank heavens. Much of humanity wants cheaper food.

title: I played for the Sydney Swans. Time will tell what the club truly values

SportAFLAFL off-field behaviour Opinion I played for the Sydney Swans. Time will tell what the club truly values Brandon Jack Commentator and author August 19, 2026 — 11:26am
